title: Roadmap 10: data access
seriesDescription: Topic-by-topic quizzes that follow the backend interview roadmap: language core, concurrency, DSA habits, web frameworks, data access, databases, messaging, resilience, security, testing, system design, and LLM/agent engineering.
description: ORM basics, lazy loading and N+1, @Transactional rules and traps, plain SQL, connection pool exhaustion, migrations, and optimistic locking in Spring and SQLAlchemy.
source: Interview roadmap study plan (Java/Spring Boot and Python/FastAPI)

questions.prompt: In SQLAlchemy 2.0 style, how do you load every User whose name is 'ana' using a Session?

options.text: session.scalars(select(User).where(User.name == 'ana')).all()
options.why: Right: select() plus scalars() is the 2.0 idiom.

options.text: User.objects.filter(name='ana').all()
options.why: That is the Django ORM, not SQLAlchemy.

options.text: session.get(User, 'ana')
options.why: get() looks up by primary key, not by an arbitrary column.

options.text: session.execute("SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = 'ana'")
options.why: 2.0 rejects bare strings; raw SQL must be wrapped in text().

questions.explanation: session.query() still works as a legacy interface, but 2.0 style builds a select() statement and runs it through session.execute() or session.scalars().

questions.prompt: An entity has `@ManyToOne(fetch = FetchType.LAZY) Customer customer`. A loop over 100 orders prints `o.getCustomer().getName()` and Hibernate logs 101 selects. What fixes it?

options.text: Load orders with `JOIN FETCH o.customer` or an @EntityGraph on the repository method.
options.why: Right: customers arrive in the same query as the orders.

options.text: Switch every association in the whole model to EAGER, so related rows always load with their parent.
options.why: EAGER over-fetches everywhere and JPQL queries can still run extra selects.

options.text: Add @Transactional to the loop so the session caches the customers.
options.why: The session cache does not batch; each uninitialised proxy still loads separately.

options.text: Raise the Hikari pool size so the 101 selects run faster.
options.why: More connections do not reduce the number of queries.

questions.explanation: Fetch what you need per use case. Hibernate's @BatchSize or hibernate.default_batch_fetch_size can turn N selects into N/size. SQLAlchemy equivalents: joinedload for to-one, selectinload for collections.

questions.prompt: True or false: `jdbc.query("select * from users where email = ?", mapper, email)` sends the email as a bind parameter, so a value like `x' OR '1'='1` is treated as plain data.

options.text: True
options.why: Right: the driver sends the statement and the value separately.

options.text: False
options.why: Placeholders are bound, not concatenated, so it is not injectable.

questions.explanation: NamedParameterJdbcTemplate uses :email placeholders in the same safe way. The unsafe version is string concatenation or f-strings. In Python use psycopg %s, asyncpg $1, or SQLAlchemy text() with :named binds.

options.text: It is ignored, because the internal call skips the Spring proxy that opens transactions.
options.why: Right: this self-invocation trap leaves save() without that transaction.

options.text: A transaction starts as normal, since the annotation is on the called method.
options.why: Annotations only work when the call goes through the proxy.

options.text: Spring fails at application startup because a public method calls another transactional method on the same bean.
options.why: Nothing is validated; the code compiles and runs silently without a transaction.

options.text: It starts a new transaction, as if propagation were REQUIRES_NEW.
options.why: The annotation is not applied at all, regardless of propagation.

questions.explanation: Fix by moving save() to another bean, putting @Transactional on placeOrder, or injecting self. Same applies to @Async, @Cacheable and @Retryable. (AspectJ mode avoids it, but proxies are the default.)

questions.prompt: Select all that apply. With default settings, which cases make a @Transactional method roll back?

options.text: An IllegalStateException propagates out of the method.
options.why: True: unchecked exceptions trigger rollback.

options.text: An AssertionError (an Error) propagates out of the method.
options.why: True: Errors roll back by default as well.

options.text: A checked IOException propagates out of the method.
options.why: False: checked exceptions commit unless rollbackFor is set.

options.text: The method catches a RuntimeException and returns normally.
options.why: False: the proxy never sees the exception, so it commits.

questions.explanation: Use rollbackFor = Exception.class when you want checked exceptions to roll back, or call TransactionAspectSupport.currentTransactionStatus().setRollbackOnly(). In SQLAlchemy, `with session.begin():` commits on a normal exit and rolls back on any exception.

questions.prompt: A Spring Boot service uses HikariCP with maximumPoolSize=10 and default timeouts. 40 requests each want a connection at once and queries are slow. What happens to the extra requests?

options.text: They wait for a free connection and fail after connectionTimeout (30 seconds by default).
options.why: Right: you see 'Connection is not available, request timed out'.

options.text: Hikari opens extra connections beyond the maximum.
options.why: The maximum is a hard cap on pool size.

options.text: They are rejected immediately with a pool-is-full error, because Hikari never makes callers wait at all.
options.why: Callers block waiting rather than being refused at once.

options.text: They queue indefinitely until a connection frees up.
options.why: The wait is bounded by connectionTimeout.

questions.explanation: Pool exhaustion usually means slow queries or connections held across slow I/O, not a pool that is too small. A bigger pool can overload Postgres; size it to the database. SQLAlchemy has the same shape: pool_size, max_overflow and pool_timeout.

questions.prompt: Two requests load the same @Version entity at version 3, change it, and save. The first commits. What happens when the second commits?

options.text: Its UPDATE ... WHERE id=? AND version=3 hits zero rows and an optimistic lock exception is thrown.
options.why: Right: the stale version is detected at write time.

options.text: It silently overwrites the first change, since the last writer wins and nothing compares the versions.
options.why: Without @Version that would happen; with it the stale write fails.

options.text: It waits on a row lock taken when the entity was loaded.
options.why: Optimistic locking takes no lock at load time.

options.text: Hibernate merges the two sets of field changes automatically.
options.why: It never merges; the caller must reload and retry.

questions.explanation: Catch ObjectOptimisticLockingFailureException, reload and retry or return 409. SQLAlchemy offers version_id_col on the mapper and raises StaleDataError.

questions.prompt: True or false: if a Flyway versioned migration V3__add_index.sql is already applied in production, it is fine to edit that file to fix a typo.

options.text: True
options.why: Editing an applied file is not safe.

options.text: False
options.why: Right: the stored checksum no longer matches, and validation fails.

questions.explanation: Flyway validates checksums and refuses to start on a mismatch. Never edit applied migrations; add V4 to correct it. Liquibase and Alembic follow the same append-only model.
